title: Why Is My Garage Door So Loud? Noise Diagnosis by Sound
description: Grinding, squeaking, or banging garage door? What each sound usually means, what you can check yourself, and when a noisy door means a real repair.
imageAlt: Wood-grain raised-panel garage door with a full hardware setup of tracks, rollers, and hinges installed on a home
keywords: noisy garage door, garage door grinding noise, garage door squeaking, garage door banging noise, why is my garage door so loud, garage door making noise when opening
h1: Why Is My Garage Door So Loud? Noise Diagnosis by Sound
intro: A garage door that's gotten noisy isn't just annoying — it's the door telling you something, and the specific sound usually points to a specific cause. A grinding door, a squeaking door, and a banging door are three different problems with three different price tags. Before you call anyone, here's how to listen to your door like a technician does: what each sound means, what's safe to check yourself, and what's a sign to stop using the door until it's looked at.

sections.heading: Squeaking or squealing: almost always dry metal
sections.body:
This is the noise we hear about most, and it's usually the least serious. A high-pitched squeak or squeal on every open and close cycle is metal-on-metal friction — rollers in their tracks, hinges pivoting between panels, or the springs themselves rotating on their shaft without enough lubrication.

**What you can check yourself:** run the door through a full cycle and listen for where the squeak gets louder — near the top (springs/shaft), along the sides (rollers/hinges), or at the header (opener chain or belt). A light coat of garage-door-specific lithium grease on the hinges, rollers, and spring coils resolves most squeaking within one or two cycles. Skip WD-40 as a long-term fix — it's a solvent that displaces old grease short-term but dries out and attracts grit, so the squeak often comes back worse within weeks.

If a fresh lubrication doesn't quiet things down within a day, the squeak is usually telling you a roller or hinge is actually worn out, not just dry — that's a straightforward repair, not an emergency.

sections.heading: Grinding or scraping: rollers, track, or bearings wearing out
sections.body:
Grinding is a rougher, lower sound than a squeak, and it usually means metal parts are actually wearing against each other rather than just needing oil. The most common causes: rollers with worn-out or flat-spotted wheels, a track that's bent or out of alignment so the roller binds instead of rolling smoothly, or worn bearings at the end of the spring shaft.

Grinding that's constant through the whole cycle points to rollers or track. Grinding concentrated at one specific point — same spot every single time the door passes it — usually means a dent or misalignment in the track at that exact location, which is worth pointing out to whoever comes to look at it.

This one is worth acting on promptly rather than waiting: a roller that's grinding because it's flat-spotted or cracked can eventually jump the track entirely, and a door that jumps its track mid-cycle can bind, jam, or drop unevenly. Roller and track repairs are typically in the standard repair range, roughly **$150 to $300**.

sections.heading: A loud bang or pop: usually a spring, and it's not optional
sections.body:
If you heard one loud bang — like a gunshot or a car backfiring — from inside the garage, and the door is now noticeably harder to lift or the opener strains and stalls partway, that's almost always a broken spring. Springs store the force that actually lifts the door (the opener just guides it), so when one lets go, it happens suddenly and loudly, and the door loses most of its lifting power in that instant.

**Stop using the door if you suspect a broken spring.** A door with a broken spring can still look like it's working — the opener may keep trying — but it's now carrying far more load than it's designed for, which stresses the opener, the remaining spring, and the cables. Look at the spring above the door (the coiled tube spanning the header): a visible gap in the coil confirms it. Spring replacement is not a do-it-yourself repair — the coils are under hundreds of pounds of tension — and typically runs **$175 to $350**, usually completed same-visit.

sections.heading: Rattling or banging on every cycle: loose hardware
sections.body:
Unlike a single loud bang, a rattle or bang that repeats on every open and close is almost always loose hardware — track brackets that have worked loose from the wall or ceiling over years of vibration, loose bolts on the hinges between panels, or a loose chain on a chain-drive opener slapping against its rail.

**What you can check yourself:** with the door closed and the opener disconnected (pull the red emergency release cord), you can safely walk the track brackets and hinge bolts with a wrench and snug anything that's visibly loose. What you shouldn't touch: anything near the spring or cable system, or the track itself if it looks bent rather than just loose — tightening bolts on a track that's actually misaligned can make the alignment worse.

sections.heading: Humming with no movement: the opener, not the door
sections.body:
If you press the button and hear the motor hum or strain but the door doesn't move — or barely twitches — that's an opener problem, not a door-hardware problem. Common causes are a stripped drive gear (a plastic gear inside the opener that wears out over years and is a known failure point on most residential openers), a capacitor going bad, or — again — a broken spring making the door too heavy for the opener to lift on its own.

Opener repairs generally run **$150 to $350** depending on the part involved; a full opener replacement starts higher and depends on the unit. Either way, this isn't a sound to keep testing repeatedly — running a straining motor over and over shortens its life and can burn it out completely.

sections.heading: When to stop and call, instead of troubleshooting further
sections.body:
Lubricating hinges and rollers, and snugging obviously loose bolts with the opener disconnected, are reasonable homeowner tasks. Everything involving the spring or cable system is not — those parts are under enough stored tension to cause serious injury if handled without the right clamps and technique.

If you've identified a sound as a single loud bang, a grinding that's gotten worse over days, or a door that's suddenly harder to lift, that's the point to stop testing it yourself and get a technician's eyes on it. faq.question: Why does my garage door make a loud grinding noise when opening?
faq.answer: Grinding usually means worn rollers, a misaligned or bent track, or worn bearings on the spring shaft — metal parts wearing against each other rather than rolling smoothly. It's worth addressing promptly, since a badly worn roller can eventually jump the track. Roller and track repairs typically run $150 to $300.

faq.question: Is it normal for a garage door to squeak?
faq.answer: Occasional light squeaking from dry hinges or rollers is common and usually fixed with garage-door-specific lithium grease on the hinges, rollers, and spring coils. If a fresh lubrication doesn't quiet it down within a day, a roller or hinge is likely actually worn out and needs replacement rather than just oil.

faq.question: I heard a loud bang from my garage — is that dangerous?
faq.answer: A single loud bang, followed by the door feeling much heavier or the opener straining, is almost always a broken spring. Stop using the door and don't attempt to replace the spring yourself — it's under hundreds of pounds of tension. Spring replacement typically costs $175 to $350 and is usually done the same day.

faq.question: My garage door opener hums but the door doesn't move — what's wrong?
faq.answer: A humming motor with little or no door movement usually points to a stripped drive gear inside the opener, a failing capacitor, or a broken spring making the door too heavy to lift. Avoid repeatedly pressing the button, since that can burn out the motor. Opener repairs generally run $150 to $350.
